title: The Surveyor's Oath to the Empty Crypt: the Ohio Country, the Continental Army, and the Power Laid Down
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Pope's Creek, the birth on the tobacco plantation
stops.date_confidence: attested. He is born 11 February 1731 by the Julian calendar then in use in the British colonies; 22 February 1732 is the Gregorian equivalent after the 1752 change, and is the date used throughout this file.
stops.campa: On a tobacco plantation above Pope's Creek in Westmoreland County, a son is born to Augustine Washington and his second wife Mary Ball, the first of their six children. The colony he is born into counts its wealth in leaf and in people, and the family holds both. He will live sixty-seven years and cross salt water exactly once. The country west of the Ohio valley he never sees at all, and almost every place he becomes famous for standing lies within four hundred miles of this creek.
suggested_refs: George Washington Birthplace National Monument, the Pope's Creek plantation site
sources: Douglas Southall Freeman, George Washington: A Biography, vol. 1

stops.name: Ferry Farm, the father's death and the first inheritance
stops.date_confidence: the move to Ferry Farm is attested to 1738 and the month and day are defaulted to 01; Augustine Washington's death is attested to 1743.
stops.campa: The family settles on the Rappahannock across from Fredericksburg, three years after moving to the Little Hunting Creek tract on the Potomac that Lawrence will rename Mount Vernon. In 1743 Augustine Washington dies, and the eleven-year-old inherits the farm and ten enslaved people. This is the first property of his life and the first term in an arithmetic that runs under all of it. The cherry tree and the dollar thrown across the river are fastened to this ground by Parson Weems sixty-eight years later, and by nobody who was there.
suggested_refs: The George Washington Foundation excavations at Ferry Farm, which located the boyhood house in 2008
sources: George Washington Foundation, Ferry Farm archaeology reports

stops.name: Culpeper County, the surveyor's oath
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: At sixteen he spends about a month in the Shenandoah Valley surveying William Fairfax's property, his first work in the field. The following year the College of William and Mary licenses him, and on the twentieth of July he swears his oath as official surveyor of Culpeper County. He is seventeen. The trade teaches him the two things he uses for the rest of his life: how to read ground before an army walks over it, and how to know precisely which acres a man owns. A federal district will be laid out by the same instruments forty-two years later.
suggested_refs: Washington's surviving field notebooks and plats from the Culpeper and Fairfax surveys, 1749-1752

stops.name: Bridgetown, the only crossing of salt water
stops.date_confidence: attested; the visit runs 2 November to 22 December 1751 by his own diary.
stops.campa: He sails with Lawrence, whose lungs are failing, to a house above Carlisle Bay, hoping the island air will do what Virginia physicians cannot. It does not. George catches smallpox instead, is laid up a month, and comes off the island lightly scarred and immune for life, which will matter in an army that loses more men to the pox than to the British. It is the only time he leaves continental North America. The diary he keeps is a young man's diary, pricing sugar and counting the guns on the batteries.
stops.quote: We were welcom'd in the House of Capt. Croftan by Capt. Crofton...
stops.quote_source: Washington's Barbados diary, 1751, ed. J. M. Toner (1892); the doubled spelling of the captain's name is the printed text's, not a transcription slip introduced here
suggested_refs: George Washington House, Bridgetown, the Bush Hill lodging above Carlisle Bay
sources: Washington's Barbados diary, 1751, ed. J. M. Toner (1892)

stops.name: Mount Vernon, the estate falls to him
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; month and day are defaulted to 01. Lawrence Washington dies in 1752, George leases the estate from his widow and inherits it outright later.
stops.campa: Lawrence dies of the disease Barbados did not cure, and the tract on Little Hunting Creek comes to his half-brother: leased first from Lawrence's widow, then held outright. Washington is twenty and has a house. For the next forty-seven years every campaign, congress, convention and administration he enters will be measured by him as an absence from this bank of the Potomac, and he will come back to it from all of them. He enlarges the house repeatedly and is never done with it before he has to leave again.
suggested_refs: The Mount Vernon mansion, in its successive enlargements of 1758-1759, 1774 and 1776-1787

stops.name: Fredericksburg, initiated Entered Apprentice
stops.date_confidence: attested in the lodge's own record
stops.campa: On the fourth of November the lodge at Fredericksburg initiates him Entered Apprentice. He is twenty. The craft he enters carries its history as a legend about Hiram Abiff, the master builder murdered at the temple of Solomon, which the craft's own nineteenth-century encyclopedist Albert Mackey will class as legend rather than fact while compiling his volumes from Washington, D.C. after 1870. The initiation is a matter of lodge record. Nearly everything later hung upon it, including an embroidered apron, is not.
suggested_refs: Fredericksburg Masonic Lodge No. 4 minute book, entry of 4 November 1752

stops.name: Logstown, the council with the Half-King
stops.date_confidence: attested in his own journal
stops.campa: Dinwiddie has sent him north with a letter ordering the French out of the Ohio Country. At the Iroquois town below the forks he sits with Tanaghrisson, the Seneca the English call the Half-King, and with the sachems of the Ohio nations, and comes away with an escort he cannot entirely trust. He is twenty-one, carrying a colony's ultimatum on the strength of his commission alone. The Iroquois name Conotocarius, town-taker, is inherited from an earlier Washington; when it was first said to his face, the sources consulted do not fix.
suggested_refs: The site of Logstown on the Ohio near present Ambridge, Pennsylvania
sources: Washington's Journal to the French Commandant on the Ohio (1754)

stops.name: Fort Le Boeuf, the ultimatum refused
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He reaches the French post in December, hands Jacques Legardeur de Saint-Pierre the governor's demand, and is fed well and refused politely. The commandant writes that he will forward the letter to Canada and will not withdraw a man. Washington counts the canoes in the yard while he waits for the answer, and rides south through winter to publish the whole exchange as a journal. The pamphlet is reprinted in London. He is not yet twenty-two and is already, on paper, a party to an imperial quarrel.
suggested_refs: The Journal of Major George Washington, Williamsburg and London printings, 1754
sources: Washington's Journal to the French Commandant on the Ohio (1754)

stops.name: Jumonville Glen, the ambush under the rocks
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: At dawn his militia and Tanaghrisson's warriors close on a French scouting party camped under the rocks. Fifteen minutes of firing, and Jumonville is dead and his party taken. What happened between the surrender and the death is disputed by the English and the French accounts and is not settled here: whether Jumonville fell in the volley or was killed afterward by Tanaghrisson with a hatchet depends on which paper one reads. The war that follows runs nine years across four continents and empties two treasuries.
suggested_refs: Jumonville Glen, the rock shelf above Chestnut Ridge, a separate site from Fort Necessity six kilometres southeast

stops.name: Fort Necessity, the only surrender
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Five weeks later the French come for him at Great Meadows with numbers he cannot meet. He has built a round stockade in a bowl of wet ground with high timber on three sides, and it rains all day into the trenches. At nightfall he signs articles of capitulation written in French, a language he does not read, containing a word that admits the assassination of Jumonville. It is the only surrender of his career, and the only document of his life he signs without knowing what it says.
suggested_refs: The reconstructed stockade at Fort Necessity National Battlefield, Great Meadows
sources: National Park Service, Fort Necessity National Battlefield

stops.name: Braddock's Field, four holes in the coat
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He rides as a volunteer aide with no command, sick with dysentery and cushioning the saddle. The column is caught in the woods short of the forks and comes apart. Braddock is shot through and dies four days later; two horses are killed under Washington and four balls go through his coat without touching him. He gathers what he can of the rear and gets it out. In Virginia the retreat makes the general ridiculous and the aide famous. His standing in this war is built out of the disasters he walks away from.
suggested_refs: Washington to his mother, 18 July 1755, in the Papers of George Washington
sources: Washington to Mary Ball Washington, 18 July 1755, Papers of George Washington

stops.name: The Forks of the Ohio, nothing left to take
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Five years after he first surveyed this junction and told Dinwiddie to fortify it, he marches in with Forbes and finds nothing to capture. The French have burned Fort Duquesne and gone down the river. He takes a brevet as brigadier general, resigns his colonial commission, and rides home to Mount Vernon and a wedding, having spent five years learning the trade at the edge of the map and lost more engagements than he won. A city grows on this point. The empire he fought for keeps the forks fifteen years.
suggested_refs: The Point at Pittsburgh, site of Fort Duquesne and its successor Fort Pitt

stops.name: Williamsburg, the seat in the House of Burgesses
stops.date_confidence: his seat runs from 1758 to 1774; the date is defaulted to the opening of the tenure rather than to any particular session.
stops.campa: He sits for Frederick County and later for Fairfax, in a chamber where the burgesses vote resolves against the taxes of a parliament three thousand miles off. He speaks rarely. Sixteen years teach him the deliberative machinery from inside it: the committees, the seconding, the patience of men who intend to be governed by consent. The men in the room are meanwhile learning what he looks like when he says nothing, and it is that, rather than anything he argued, they remember about him in Philadelphia in 1775.
suggested_refs: The Capitol at the east end of Duke of Gloucester Street, Williamsburg, seat of the House of Burgesses
sources: Journals of the House of Burgesses of Virginia

stops.name: New Kent County, the marriage to Martha Custis
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He marries Martha Dandridge Custis, widow, at twenty-six. She brings the largest fortune he will ever handle and eighty-four people held in the Custis dower estate, whom he will manage for forty years and be unable to free, because they were never his to free. The wedding remakes his finances: after it he is not a soldier angling for a regular commission but one of the wealthier planters in Virginia. The limits on the will he writes at the end of his life are set on this day.
suggested_refs: The White House plantation on the Pamunkey, New Kent County, site of the January 1759 wedding

stops.name: Mount Vernon, out of tobacco and into wheat
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; month and day are defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He takes the estate out of tobacco and puts it into wheat, builds a mill to grind it and a cooperage to barrel it, and adds hemp. Tobacco was sold through London factors who set the price, kept the accounts and held the debt; wheat can be sold in the West Indies for cash. Four years later, on the Ohio and the Great Kanawha, William Crawford surveys him twenty-three thousand two hundred acres of bounty land. He is turning himself from a consignment planter into a man with his own markets, a decade before the political argument.
suggested_refs: The gristmill and distillery at Dogue Run, Mount Vernon, reconstructed on the excavated foundations

stops.name: Carpenters' Hall, the First Continental Congress
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Congress sits from 5 September to 26 October 1774.
stops.campa: He rides to Philadelphia as one of Virginia's delegates, having drafted the Fairfax Resolves with George Mason that summer, a document that condemns the Atlantic slave trade in the same breath as the taxes. In the hall he meets for the first time most of the men he will spend the next twenty-five years commanding, arguing with and governing beside. He is the only delegate present who arrives with a soldier's reputation, and he does not press it in the debates.
suggested_refs: The Fairfax Resolves, adopted 18 July 1774, drafted with George Mason

segments.name: The Command and the Losing Year

stops.name: The Pennsylvania State House, elected commander-in-chief
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Congress makes a Continental Army out of the militia camped around Boston and elects him its commander-in-chief without a dissenting vote. The choice is partly geography: a Virginian at the head of a New England war binds in the colonies that have not yet bled. Accepting the next day, he declines any salary and asks that his expenses be paid. He is forty-three, has never commanded more than a regiment, has never won a campaign, and has been out of uniform for sixteen years.
suggested_refs: The Assembly Room of the Pennsylvania State House, where the vote of 15 June 1775 was taken
sources: Journals of the Continental Congress, 15 June 1775

stops.name: Cambridge, the Vassall House and the siege of Boston
stops.date_confidence: he holds this headquarters from July 1775 to April 1776; the day is defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He takes command in a Brattle Street mansion abandoned by a loyalist and finds an army that is not one: militia companies that elect their own officers, enlist for months, and go home at harvest. He spends the siege on paperwork, which is the work here: returns, rations, and powder counts that show he has almost none. The British sit in Boston all winter without discovering it. In this house he settles into the work of keeping a force in existence, and for six years he will do almost nothing else.
suggested_refs: The Vassall House on Brattle Street, later Longfellow's, now Longfellow House-Washington's Headquarters
sources: National Park Service, Longfellow House-Washington's Headquarters National Historic Site

stops.name: Dorchester Heights, the guns from Ticonderoga
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In one night his men raise fortifications on the heights above the harbour, mounting cannon that Henry Knox has dragged three hundred miles on sledges from Ticonderoga. In the morning Howe looks up at guns that can reach his fleet and decides not to fight for the town. On the seventeenth the British sail for Halifax. Not a shot is fired from the position. No engagement of his war costs him less. It is won by oxen on sledges and by one night's digging in frozen ground.
suggested_refs: Knox's noble train of artillery, Ticonderoga to Cambridge, December 1775 to January 1776

stops.name: Brooklyn Heights, the army taken off the island
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Howe returns with the largest expeditionary force Britain has ever sent anywhere and takes Long Island in a day, turning the American left through a pass nobody was watching. Washington loses the battle, and then on the night of the twenty-ninth takes his whole army off the island across the East River in fog, boat by boat, without losing a man. Manhattan goes next, and Fort Washington in November, and by December he is retreating through New Jersey with five thousand four hundred men.
suggested_refs: The East River evacuation of 29-30 August 1776, from the Brooklyn ferry landing to Manhattan

stops.name: McConkey's Ferry, the crossing of the Delaware
stops.date_confidence: attested; the crossing runs through the night of 25-26 December 1776.
stops.campa: On Christmas night he puts roughly two thousand four hundred men, with horses and eighteen guns, into Durham boats and across a river running ice. The enlistments of most of them expire in six days. Two supporting columns fail to get over; his crosses, three hours behind schedule, and marches nine miles through sleet to be in position by dawn. Seventy-five years later Emanuel Leutze will paint the scene with the wrong boat, the wrong flag and the general standing up. The night itself is a logistics problem solved in the dark.
suggested_refs: The Pennsylvania bank at Washington Crossing, embarkation point of the night of 25 December 1776

stops.name: Trenton, the Hessian garrison taken
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Hessian garrison is taken in about forty-five minutes on a snowing morning, eight hundred and ninety-six prisoners marched off and almost no American dead. The tactical value is small. The political value is the war: a cause that has been losing since August has won something, and men whose enlistments expire on the thirty-first agree to stay six weeks longer when he rides down the line and asks them. He pays their bounty with money he has no authority to promise.
suggested_refs: The Old Barracks, Trenton, and the Hessian regiments Rall, Lossberg and Knyphausen

stops.name: Princeton, between the firing lines
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Slipping around Cornwallis in the night with the campfires left burning, he strikes the British rear at Princeton and rides into the gap himself when the militia starts to break, sitting his horse between two firing lines while his own men close up behind him. The battle ends with an artillery duel against redcoats sheltering in Nassau Hall. In ten days he has taken Trenton twice and Princeton once, and the British give up the Delaware valley for the winter.
suggested_refs: The Thomas Clarke farm on the Princeton battlefield, where the militia was rallied

stops.name: Brandywine Creek, the Frenchman shot through the calf
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Howe turns his right the way he turned his left on Long Island, and Washington loses again, this time with Philadelphia at his back. A nineteen-year-old volunteer major general, the Marquis de Lafayette, is shot through the calf and stays on the field until Washington sends a surgeon with orders to treat him as though he were his son. The wound becomes Lafayette's credential with Congress and with the army. Washington is forty-five and childless, and has acquired the nearest thing to a son he will have.
stops.quote: Although he was surrounded by officers and citizens, it was impossible to mistake for a moment his majestic figure and deportment; nor was he less distinguished by the noble affability of his manner.
stops.quote_source: Marquis de Lafayette, Memoirs, Correspondence, and Manuscripts of General Lafayette, vol. 1 (Project Gutenberg 8376), recalling his first sight of Washington at a Philadelphia dinner earlier in 1777
suggested_refs: Chadds Ford and the fords of the Brandywine, 11 September 1777

stops.name: Valley Forge, the winter and the cabal
stops.date_confidence: the encampment is attested from December 1777 to June 1778; the day is defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The army winters eighteen miles from a Philadelphia full of British officers, in huts it builds itself, on a supply system that has collapsed. Baron von Steuben arrives in February and drills the whole force to a single manual of arms in a language he does not speak, through translators. In the same months the Conway Cabal moves to replace the commander-in-chief and offers the command to Lafayette, who refuses it flat. The army that marches out in June can maneuver, and it is still his.
stops.quote: I have not sought for this place; if I am displeasing to the nation I will retire; but until then I will oppose all intrigues.
stops.quote_source: Quoted as Washington's own words in Lafayette's account of the Conway Cabal, Memoirs, Correspondence, and Manuscripts of General Lafayette, vol. 1 (Project Gutenberg 8376)
suggested_refs: The Isaac Potts house at Valley Forge, Washington's headquarters through the winter of 1777-1778
sources: National Park Service, Valley Forge National Historical Park

stops.name: Monmouth Court House, the question put to Charles Lee
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Chasing the British across New Jersey in murderous heat, he finds Charles Lee's advance corps retreating without orders and rides into the middle of it. What he said to Lee is on the record and is a question, twice over, about reason and disorder and confusion. What the tradition adds is that he swore until the leaves shook on the trees, a line that comes from Charles Scott long afterward and belongs to the legend rather than the papers. He reforms the line himself and holds the field. Lafayette holds his ground until it is reformed.
stops.quote: I desire to know, sir, what is the reason - whence arises this disorder and confusion?
stops.quote_source: Washington to Charles Lee on the field at Monmouth, 28 June 1778, Papers of George Washington, Revolutionary War Series, vol. 15
suggested_refs: The Monmouth battlefield in Manalapan and Freehold Township, distinct from Freehold Borough four kilometres east
sources: Papers of George Washington, Revolutionary War Series, vol. 15

stops.name: Yorktown, the sword nobody accepts
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Lafayette pins Cornwallis against the coast, de Grasse's fleet closes the bay, Rochambeau's regiments come down from the north, and the silver that pays the French fleet was raised in Havana, where Francisco de Miranda works in Cagigal's counting-houses. The treasury of Louis XVI has bought this field, eight years before the scaffold. When O'Hara offers the sword of surrender, Rochambeau declines it and points to Washington, and Washington declines it and points to Benjamin Lincoln. Nobody in the ceremony takes what is handed him.
suggested_refs: The surrender field at Yorktown, 19 October 1781, and the terms denying the British the honours of war
sources: Papers of George Washington, Revolutionary War Series, vol. 33

stops.name: New Windsor Cantonment, the spectacles
stops.date_confidence: attested. The address is delivered at the New Building of the cantonment, not at his Newburgh residence at Hasbrouck House, which he holds from April 1782 to August 1783.
stops.campa: Peace is coming and the army has not been paid, and an anonymous address circulates among the officers proposing that they refuse to disband until Congress settles with them. Washington walks into the meeting uninvited, takes out a written answer, and then takes out a pair of spectacles that almost none of them has ever seen him wear. He asks their permission to put them on. The mutiny ends in the sentence that follows it, and the officers vote their confidence in Congress the same hour.
stops.quote: you will permit me to put on my spectacles, for I have not only grown gray but almost blind in the service of my country
stops.quote_source: Washington to the assembled officers at the New Building, New Windsor Cantonment, 15 March 1783
suggested_refs: The New Building, or Temple, at the New Windsor Cantonment; and Hasbrouck House, Newburgh, his longest-held headquarters
sources: Washington's address to the officers, 15 March 1783

stops.name: Fraunces Tavern, farewell in the Long Room
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Nine days after the British sail out of New York he says goodbye to his officers in the Long Room of a tavern near the water, embracing each of them in turn, and none of the men present can afterward describe it without breaking off. Some of these officers have founded the Society of the Cincinnati and made him its president, a hereditary order of veterans named for a Roman who went back to his plough. A city on the Ohio will take its name from that order, and a young man named John Cleves Symmes will ride west through it.
suggested_refs: The Long Room of Fraunces Tavern at Pearl and Broad Streets, and the Society of the Cincinnati founded May 1783

stops.name: Annapolis, the commission handed back
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He walks into the chamber of the Confederation Congress, reads a short paper, hands back the commission he received in Philadelphia in June 1775, and goes home. He is fifty-one and has held supreme military command for eight and a half years over an army that was frequently unpaid and occasionally the only functioning institution in the country. European observers accustomed to victorious generals keeping their armies have no category for the act. He rides for the Potomac and reaches Mount Vernon on Christmas Eve.
suggested_refs: The Old Senate Chamber of the Maryland State House, Annapolis, 23 December 1783
sources: Journals of the Continental Congress, 23 December 1783

stops.name: Mount Vernon, the embroidered apron
stops.date_confidence: the gift is placed in 1784 by the Mount Vernon provenance records and by the Lafayette journeys; month and day are defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: John Rutledge Jr. carries a Masonic apron across the Atlantic, embroidered, sent by Lafayette. The tradition that Adrienne de Lafayette and her daughters worked it is carried in the Mount Vernon provenance and in Lafayette's own family record. The Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania, which received an apron by the transfer of 1829, later withdrew that attribution in its own museum record. Two aprons, or one, or a family story: the needlework crossed the ocean, and the question of whose hands made it did not close.
suggested_refs: The Washington Masonic apron in the collection of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania, and the 1829 transfer record

stops.name: Mount Vernon, the conference in his dining room
stops.date_confidence: attested; the commissioners sit from 25 to 28 March 1785.
stops.campa: Commissioners from Virginia and Maryland come to his dining room for four days to settle who may fish, ferry and navigate the Potomac, and they settle it. Two states have treated with each other successfully while no government exists that could have made them, and the men who want such a government take the point. The meeting leads to Annapolis the next year and to Philadelphia the year after. He has spent the previous autumn surveying canal works at the Great Falls for the same reason. The west has to be tied on by water.
suggested_refs: The Mount Vernon Conference of March 1785 and the Potowmack Company works at the Great Falls
sources: Mount Vernon Ladies' Association, Mount Vernon Conference records

stops.name: Mount Vernon, the life mask and the Milanese guest
stops.date_confidence: attested by Washington's own diary; Houdon's visit falls in October of the same year.
stops.campa: In October the sculptor Jean-Antoine Houdon comes from Paris, lays plaster on his face for a life mask, and measures his arms, legs, hands and chest; the marble that results will stand in Richmond from 1796, in uniform, beside a plough and a bundle of rods. At Christmas the Milanese naturalist Luigi Castiglioni arrives for dinner and stays four days. In one season a sculptor writes down his body and a traveller writes down his bearing. Castiglioni puts his age at fifty-seven. He is fifty-three.
stops.quote: General Washington is perhaps fifty-seven years of age, a man large and strong of build, of a majestic but kindly bearing, and, notwithstanding the fatigues of war, appears not yet to be aging.
stops.quote_source: Count Luigi Castiglioni, Viaggio negli Stati Uniti, in Travels in Virginia in Revolutionary Times, ed. Alfred J. Morrison (1922), Project Gutenberg 63221; the translator of the excerpt is not identified in that edition, and Washington was in fact fifty-three
suggested_refs: Houdon's marble Washington in the rotunda of the Virginia State Capitol, Richmond, delivered 1796
sources: Travels in Virginia in Revolutionary Times, ed. Alfred J. Morrison (1922)

stops.name: Independence Hall, presiding in near silence
stops.date_confidence: attested; the convention sits from 25 May to 17 September 1787.
stops.campa: The convention elects him its president on the first day, and he presides for four months, speaking almost never. Farrand's records of the debates show how little of the argument is his. The delegates design a single executive with real powers, and they design it in a room that contains the man everyone expects to hold the office first. He signs the document in September and rides home. Nine months later the ratifying conventions have made the office real, and there is only one name in anybody's mouth to fill it.
suggested_refs: Max Farrand, Records of the Federal Convention of 1787
sources: Max Farrand, Records of the Federal Convention of 1787

stops.name: Federal Hall, the first oath
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Electoral College is unanimous, which will not happen again for anyone. He takes the oath on a balcony over Wall Street in a suit of brown American broadcloth, and every act of the office afterward is a precedent, because there is nothing behind it to consult. The words so help me God, fastened to this oath in the American memory, appear first in Washington Irving's biography of 1859; the newspaper accounts printed at the time do not carry them. He is fifty-seven and has been retired for sixteen months.
suggested_refs: The balcony of Federal Hall on Wall Street, 30 April 1789; contemporary newspaper accounts of the oath
sources: Washington Irving, Life of Washington, vol. 5 (1859)

stops.name: Mount Vernon, the key of the Bastille
stops.date_confidence: the gift is placed in 1790 by the Lafayette journey; month and day are defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Lafayette has the main key of the demolished Bastille sent across the Atlantic, carried by Thomas Paine, a gift from one revolution to the man the other one learned from. Washington hangs it in the passage of the house, and it hangs there still. In the same decade the Lafayettes' son, named George Washington Lafayette, is sent out of the Terror across the ocean and lives under this roof while his father is in an Austrian prison and his mother Adrienne is in a French one.
stops.quote: General Washington never placed unlimited confidence in any person, except in M. de Lafayette; because for him alone, perhaps, confidence sprung from warm affection.
stops.quote_source: Lafayette characterising Washington's trust in him, written in the third person for the editorial framing of Memoirs, Correspondence, and Manuscripts of General Lafayette, vol. 1 (Project Gutenberg 8376)
suggested_refs: The Bastille key in its case in the central passage at Mount Vernon

stops.name: The President's House on Market Street, Philadelphia
stops.date_confidence: the residence runs from November 1790 to March 1797; the day is defaulted to 01. The Seneca address is of December 1790 and Oney Judge leaves on 21 May 1796.
stops.campa: The government sits in Philadelphia for a decade while a federal city is built on the Potomac. Pennsylvania's gradual abolition law frees any enslaved person held in the state above six months, so nine people from Mount Vernon are rotated back across the state line before the clock runs out, again and again, for six years. On the twenty-first of May 1796 Oney Judge walks out of this house and does not come back. In December 1790 the Seneca chiefs Cornplanter, Half-Town and Great-Tree come to it to speak.
stops.quote: Father: The voice of the Seneca Nations speaks to you, the great counsellor, in whose heart the wise men of all the Thirteen Fires have placed their wisdom; it may be very small in your ears, and we therefore entreat you to hearken with attention, for we are about to speak of things which are to us very great.
stops.quote_source: Cornplanter, Half-Town and Great-Tree to President Washington, December 1790; text as printed at sullivanclinton.com, flagged in the report for re-verification against American State Papers, Indian Affairs, vol. 1, Founders Online being unreachable in this session
suggested_refs: The President's House site at Sixth and Market, Philadelphia, and the memorial to the nine enslaved members of the household
sources: Edward Lawler Jr., 'The President's House in Philadelphia', Pennsylvania Magazine of History and Biography (2002)

stops.name: Fort Cumberland, the militia mustered against the whiskey counties
stops.date_confidence: October 1794 is attested; the day is defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Western Pennsylvania will not pay the excise on whiskey, so he federalises the militia and rides out at its head to the muster at Wills Creek, the same staging ground he used against the French in 1755 and again in 1758. No battle is fought and the rebellion evaporates in front of the column. It is the only occasion on which a sitting President has taken the field in command of troops, and he does it to collect a tax, on the ground where he first learned how a campaign is lost.
suggested_refs: Fort Cumberland at Wills Creek, staging ground of the Braddock and Forbes campaigns and of the 1794 muster
sources: Papers of George Washington, Presidential Series, vol. 17

stops.name: Philadelphia, the Farewell Address printed
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He publishes his refusal of a third term in Claypoole's American Daily Advertiser rather than delivering it, so that it reaches the country as a newspaper column and not as a speech from a throne. Hamilton has done most of the drafting on his instructions, over an outline Madison made in 1792. It warns against permanent foreign alliances and against the spirit of party, six and a half weeks before the polls open in the first contested presidential election, which the parties win. Congress will read it aloud on his birthday for two centuries.
suggested_refs: Claypoole's American Daily Advertiser, 19 September 1796; the annual Senate reading and its leather-bound journal

segments.name: The Vault and the Empty Crypt

stops.name: Mount Vernon, the throat closes
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He rides the farms on the thirteenth in snow and freezing rain, comes in wet, and will not keep dinner waiting to change. By the next night his throat has closed. He is bled four times with his own consent, losing a great quantity of blood, and dies at ten in the evening with Tobias Lear holding his wrist and counting the pulse. What killed him is argued still: epiglottitis, quinsy, the bleedings themselves. Lear's account records the symptoms and no diagnosis, because there was none available to make.
suggested_refs: Tobias Lear's account of Washington's last illness, 14 December 1799
sources: Tobias Lear, account of Washington's death, 14 December 1799

stops.name: Mount Vernon, the old family vault
stops.date_confidence: attested; four days after death, not three as some accounts state.
stops.campa: He is laid in the family vault four days later, a brick chamber already decaying when he inherited it, and his will directs that a new one be built on a site he designates himself. The same will frees his valet William Lee outright, and provides for the manumission at Martha's death of the one hundred and twenty-four people he owned. It has no power over the hundred and fifty-three Custis dower slaves at Mount Vernon, nor the forty who are rented. Martha signs the deed in December 1800 and it takes effect on the first of January 1801.
suggested_refs: Washington's last will and testament, and the 1799 Mount Vernon slave census listing 317 people in three categories
sources: George Washington's last will and testament

stops.name: Mount Vernon, Lafayette alone with the coffin
stops.date_confidence: the visit is placed in 1824 by the Lafayette journey; month and day are defaulted to 01, and the October date of the tour itinerary is not carried into this field.
stops.campa: Forty-one years after Annapolis, on his tour of the country he helped make, Lafayette asks to be left alone in the vault, and comes out weeping. He carries away a ring cut from Washington's hair. He will be buried at Picpus in Paris under earth brought from Bunker Hill. The son who was sheltered in this house during the Terror is travelling with him. The calf wound at Brandywine and the surgeon sent across the field with an order about a son are forty-seven years behind them both.
suggested_refs: Lafayette's 1824-1825 tour of the United States and his visit to the Mount Vernon tomb

stops.name: Mount Vernon, the new tomb built at last
stops.date_confidence: the tomb is built in 1831; month and day are defaulted to 01. The sarcophagus is installed 7 October 1837.
stops.campa: In 1830 somebody breaks into the old vault to take the skull and fails, and the family finally builds the brick tomb the will had specified thirty-two years before. The coffins are moved. In 1837 the lead inner casket goes into a marble sarcophagus cut by John Struthers of Philadelphia and set to the right of the iron gate, with Martha's on the left. From here the grave is a destination rather than a burial. The Mount Vernon Ladies' Association takes the estate in 1858 and has not let it close since.
suggested_refs: The new tomb at Mount Vernon, 1831, and the Struthers sarcophagi installed 7 October 1837

stops.name: The United States Capitol, the crypt that stayed empty
stops.date_confidence: the crypt is built under Bulfinch in the 1820s and the estate's refusal is dated 1832; the flat 1827 completion date given in the research pool is not supported and is not used here.
stops.campa: A tomb for him was drawn into William Thornton's design for the Capitol, and the chamber was built beneath the rotunda in the 1820s. It was never filled. The design and its cost were disputed, the will bound him to Mount Vernon, Martha had assented to that, and in 1832 John Augustine Washington refused to release the remains. The crypt became a corridor holding statuary and the compass point from which the city's four quadrants are measured. Miranda came to this capital in 1783 to study him, Alvear presented credentials here in 1824, Tschiffely rode into it in 1928. The body never arrived.
suggested_refs: Washington's Tomb beneath the Capitol rotunda, and the compass stone marking the origin of the District's quadrants
